newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - FTSE 100 expiry prompts heavy volume.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FTSE 100 expiry prompts heavy volume.

text.p: The UK traded options market was active on Friday as dealers scrambled to cover short positions in FTSE 100 index contracts which expired this morning.
"There were a lot of people short of the January FTSE 4,200 calls," one dealer said.

"The bulls won the day which pushed the FTSE futures and the cash market higher. Once the contract expired, the FTSE cash market drifted back down to a level it probably should have been at all along."
The FTSE 100 index was up 2.0 points at 4,199.5 by 1230 GMT after hitting a record high of 4,218.4 earlier in the session.
Dealers said over 31,000 FTSE 100 options contracts had been traded by midday, including nearly 11,000 February 4,350 calls.
"There has been a lot of call spreading going on in February (contracts). February out-of-the money calls are being sold heavily," said one.

Amongst individual shares, a bearish put spread was established in British Petroleum Plc when one dealer sold 1,000 BP April 650 puts at 8p and then bought 1,000 April 700 puts at 23-1/2p, for a net debit of 15-1/2p, plus commissions.
A maximum profit would be realised if BP shares were below 650p at the time of expiration.
The maximum risk is limited to the 15-1/2p debit and would be triggered if BP shares were anywhere above 700p at expiration. BP shares were down 2-1/2p at 712p.

A synthetic long was set up in Vodafone when one dealer sold 1,000 April 240 puts at 5p and then bought 1,000 April 280 calls at 6-1/2p. Splitting the strikes gives the dealer some room for error, while still retaining the potential for large profits. Vodafone was down 5p at 255p.
If Vodafone shares rise far enough, a profit will be made on both the call and the put. If the share remains stable, the call will expire at a loss but the put sale will be in profit.
